Adverse possession in Tennessee

A person can gain legal title, or a defense to the owner's lawsuit, only by meeting a demanding test over a long stretch of time. The possession must be exclusive, actual, adverse, continuous, open and notorious for the period the law requires. In 2024 the Tennessee Supreme Court spelled out what the adversity part of that test takes.

The rules sit in Tenn. Code Ann. Title 28, chapter 2, part 1, alongside a body of common law. The time periods and the exceptions are technical, so an owner facing a real claim should get the parcel's facts in front of a Tennessee attorney early.

A person who simply moves into a vacant house, or who stays after permission ends, is not automatically on the road to ownership. The next section explains why adversity is the sticking point.

The Mathes v. 99 Hermitage decision

The Court held that adversity, for both common-law and statutory adverse possession, requires either a conflict of title or a controversy about the right to possess the property. The opinion was issued July 31, 2024, in a case that began in chancery court.

The facts show how a real owner can still end up in a possession fight. A buyer obtained legal title to a commercial property near downtown Nashville but did not register the deed. About twenty years later, the person who had sold the property to him defaulted on a loan, and the lender's judgment lien led to a sale. The plaintiffs argued the buyer had adversely possessed the property during the gap. The Court rejected that argument because neither a title conflict nor a possession dispute existed for the required time.

  • An unregistered deed sat in the chain while the seller's creditor pursued the property.
  • Long, quiet use of land does not by itself satisfy the adversity element.
  • The opinion reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the chancery court's judgment.

The practical lesson is to record every deed promptly with the county register of deeds. The fee in Davidson County starts at a $10 minimum plus a $2 data processing fee, which is small next to the risk that buyer carried.

Removing someone who has no right to be there

The route is a detainer warrant in general sessions court. Tennessee law recognizes three types under Title 29, chapter 18: forcible entry and detainer (29-18-102), forcible detainer (29-18-103) and unlawful detainer (29-18-104). Which one fits depends on how the person came to be in the house, such as a tenant who stayed past the lease or an occupant who entered without permission.

A summons can be served on any adult found in possession of the premises, and service on that person is enough to let the owner regain the property. When nobody is found, the court system's training materials describe a posting route. The plaintiff first tries personal service on three different dates and writes each attempt on the face of the warrant. After the third failed attempt, the plaintiff posts a copy on the door, mails the warrant and makes a note on the warrant. The posting has to go up at least six days before the hearing.

Detainer warrant timing in Tennessee general sessions court
StepRule or deadline
Service on an occupantSummons may be served on any adult found in possession
Service by postingThree attempts on different dates, then door posting, mailing and a notation, at least six days before the hearing
ContinuanceFifteen days at most, unless the parties agree, the landlord consents or no court is being held
Writ of possessionExecuted immediately once awarded after judgment for the plaintiff
Appeal to circuit courtTen days under Tenn. Code Ann. 27-5-108
Certiorari and supersedeasThirty days, with a bond and a stated meritorious reason

If the occupant appeals the judgment

The bond rule favors a plaintiff who has already won. A defendant who appeals must post a bond covering one year of rent. If the defendant skips that bond, the plaintiff does not have to post a bond of its own to obtain possession. The plaintiff is entitled to interest on the judgment, running from the judgment date, if the appeal fails.

When the defendant does post the bond, the plaintiff must execute a bond in double the value of one year's rent, conditioned on paying costs and damages from any wrongful enforcement of the writ. A defendant who seeks circuit court review by certiorari must post a bond covering costs and damages, and when the defendant is the applicant the bond must also cover rent during the litigation.

An attorney handles these procedural details, but they explain why a contested removal can run longer than the first hearing suggests. If you plan to sell, build that extra time into your listing or closing date.

Who carries out the removal?

The county sheriff executes the writ. A writ of restitution is not executed until the sheriff delivers actual possession of the premises to the plaintiff and leaves the plaintiff in quiet possession. If the occupant refuses to leave, removing the person is the officer's duty, and Tenn. Code Ann. 29-18-127 authorizes force where needed.

  • The officer oversees the procedure and keeps the peace. Officers should not act as the plaintiff's movers.
  • The plaintiff is responsible for removing and storing the occupant's belongings.
  • Hazardous items, such as weapons or prescription medications, are to be inventoried and secured.
  • Entering the wrong residence is a recurring source of lawsuits, so check the address on the writ against the parcel.

Never change locks or remove an occupant's belongings on your own authority. The court process exists so that the sheriff, not the owner, performs the removal.

When the occupant is a former tenant

Different rules can apply. Tennessee has two landlord-tenant regimes. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies in Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Greene, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Putnam, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson counties. Every other county falls under Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-101 and following.

Under URLTA the notices run fourteen, seven or three days, depending on the violation, with a five-day grace period on rent. Outside URLTA counties the notices are fourteen-day, thirty-day and three-day. Written notice is required, and the owner must rely in court on the reasons stated in the notice. If new misconduct occurs after the notice, a new notice is needed.

A buyer or a title company will ask who lives in the house and on what terms. A clean court record of a completed detainer case answers that better than a verbal promise to leave.

Selling an occupied or disputed house

Start by establishing who holds title. Pull the recorded deed, confirm the owner of record in the register of deeds' office, and make sure no gap like the one in Mathes exists in your chain. If a stranger claims an interest, expect a title company to require that claim to be resolved before closing.

  • Gather the recorded deed and any loan or lien paperwork.
  • Write down when the occupant arrived and whether you ever gave permission.
  • Keep copies of notices, texts and rent records.
  • File the detainer warrant in the general sessions court of the county where the house sits.

Some buyers who purchase as-is will take an occupied property, but the occupant's situation will shape the price and the timeline. Describe the facts plainly when you ask for an offer.

Frequently asked questions

Can a squatter take my Tennessee house?

Only through adverse possession, which requires exclusive, actual, adverse, continuous, open and notorious possession for the period the law sets. The Tennessee Supreme Court held in 2024 that adversity requires a conflict of title or a controversy over the right to possess.

How do I remove an occupant who is not a tenant?

File a detainer warrant in general sessions court. Tennessee recognizes forcible entry and detainer, forcible detainer and unlawful detainer under Tenn. Code Ann. 29-18-102 through 29-18-104.

Can I change the locks myself?

No. Removal is carried out by the sheriff under a writ, and the writ is not executed until the sheriff delivers actual possession to the plaintiff.

How long do I have to appeal a general sessions detainer ruling?

Ten days under Tenn. Code Ann. 27-5-108. A separate route, certiorari and supersedeas to circuit court, must be sought within thirty days and requires a bond.

What if I cannot find the person to serve?

After three documented attempts on different dates, the plaintiff may post the warrant on the door, mail it and note the steps on the warrant, at least six days before the hearing. Posting supports possession but not a money judgment.

Tennessee Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Which Tennessee counties follow the URLTA

Only the larger counties follow it. The act, found in Title 66, Chapter 28 of the Tennessee Code, reaches counties with more than 75,000 residents by the 2010 federal census. Nineteen counties qualify: Shelby, Davidson, Knox, Hamilton, Rutherford, Williamson, Montgomery, Sumner, Wilson, Blount, Sullivan, Washington, Bradley, Sevier, Madison, Maury, Anderson, Greene and Putnam.

The remaining counties fall under Title 66, Chapter 7 of the Code, starting at section 101. Only four sections of that older law actually apply: section 109 on termination of tenancy, 110 on tenants with disabilities, 111 on service and support animals, and 112 on domestic abuse.

How the two Tennessee landlord tenant regimes differ.
TopicURLTA countiesAll other counties
Governing lawTitle 66, Chapter 28Title 66, Chapter 7 (four sections apply)
Rent grace periodFive days, not counting Sundays and legal holidaysNot covered by those four sections
Late fee cap10 percent of the rent past dueNot covered by those four sections
Notice types14 day, 7 day for repeat violations, 3 day14 day, 30 day, 3 day

Check which column your rental belongs in before you send any notice or promise any date. The county clerk or a local attorney can confirm it.

Written notices a Tennessee landlord sends

In a URLTA county, a landlord facing a material breach can deliver written notice that the lease ends after 14 days unless the tenant cures the problem. A repeat of substantially the same act or omission inside six months permits a seven day written notice. Section 66-28-505 sets out these steps, and a three day notice also exists for violence, threats and unsanitary conditions.

  • Monthly tenancy: either party ends it by written notice delivered at least 30 days before the rent due date the notice specifies (section 66-28-512).
  • Weekly tenancy: written notice delivered at least ten days before the end date.
  • Tenant repairs to cure a breach need a written request from the tenant and written authorization from the landlord before work begins.
  • A holdover who remains without consent once the term ends is open to a suit for possession, back rent and reasonable attorney fees.

The owner must rely on the reasons stated in the notice when the case reaches court. New misconduct after a notice goes out calls for another notice. Subsidized housing requires written notice, and federal rules may differ from state law.

What happens to a lease if the landlord sells the house?

The statute deals with the seller's liability and does not end a tenancy. Section 66-28-305 releases a landlord who conveys to a bona fide purchaser in good faith from liability for later events, once the tenant has written notice of the conveyance and the security deposit has moved to the purchaser. Skip either step and the seller stays exposed.

Section 66-28-302 obliges a landlord to give the tenant who manages the property and who may receive service and notices for the owner, with an address for each. The same section makes that duty enforceable against any successor landlord, owner or manager, so whoever buys a rented house takes on that duty.

  • Tell the tenant in writing that the property changed hands and where the deposit now sits.
  • Hand over to the buyer the lease, the deposit and the tenant's contact details.
  • Call the county clerk or a local attorney to learn what notice your lease and county require before assuming the sale lets you end the lease.

Showings come with limits. Section 66-28-403 says a tenant should not unreasonably refuse entry so the landlord can exhibit the unit to actual or prospective buyers, while barring abuse of that access. The same section lists the only situations in which a landlord may enter without consent, such as an emergency or a court order.

Security deposits

Section 66-28-301 requires URLTA-county landlords to place each deposit in an account used only for deposits, at a bank or lender regulated by Tennessee or the federal government. Tenants learn where the account is when they sign and pay, though the account number stays private.

  • Tenants may inspect the unit for the damage behind any charge, and the landlord may invite them to attend.
  • A landlord who skipped the separate account or the written damage listing may not keep any of the deposit.
  • Damage found later is recoverable only if the landlord spotted it inside 30 days after the tenant left or inside seven days after a new tenant took possession, whichever ends first.
  • When nothing is owed and a refund is due, the landlord sends a refund notice to the tenant's last known address, and if no reply arrives within 60 days the landlord may take the money out of the account.

A seller has to pass the deposit to the buyer to earn the release described above. Put the amount in the closing paperwork so both sides agree on it. A cash buyer who takes the house with the tenant in place receives the lease and the deposit the same way.

How an eviction case moves through court

A landlord files a detainer warrant in general sessions court. Three types exist: forcible entry and detainer under section 29-18-102, forcible detainer under 29-18-103 and unlawful detainer under 29-18-104.

  • Service: the summons can go to any adult found in possession, or to a party named in the lease. Personal service supports a money judgment.
  • Posting: after three attempts on three different dates, documented on the warrant, service can be made by posting a copy on the door and mailing one, at least six days before the hearing. Posting supports possession only, not a money judgment.
  • Continuances: the maximum is 15 days unless the parties agree, the landlord consents, or no court is being held.
  • Appeal: a defendant has ten days to appeal to circuit court and must post bond. A certiorari route to circuit court runs 30 days and needs a meritorious reason and bond.
  • Writ of possession: when the landlord wins, the writ is executed and the landlord restored to possession immediately.

If a defendant appeals without posting the required bond, the landlord does not have to post one to obtain possession. The landlord is also entitled to interest on the judgment from the judgment date if the defendant's appeal fails.

Protections for domestic abuse victims in a rental

The URLTA and the older law use identical wording, in sections 66-28-205 and 66-28-517 for URLTA counties and 66-7-109 and 66-7-112 elsewhere. If domestic abuse is the reason a tenancy could be ended, only the perpetrator may be evicted. The landlord may not evict the victim, minor children or innocent occupants, and the perpetrator stays financially liable.

A landlord may remove the perpetrator from the lease and have the remaining adult tenants qualify for a new agreement. The victim and the other adult tenants must agree in writing not to let the perpetrator return. A tenant who is a domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking victim can also request release from the lease by written notice, with a release date agreed within 30 days and a copy of either a valid order of protection after a hearing or documents showing a criminal charge.

A seller whose tenancy involves an order of protection should get legal advice before serving any notice.

Frequently asked questions

Does the URLTA apply in my Tennessee county?

It applies in counties with more than 75,000 residents under the 2010 census. Nineteen counties qualify, including Davidson, Shelby, Knox, Hamilton and Rutherford. If your county is not listed, the shorter Title 66, Chapter 7 law applies, so confirm with your county clerk before sending notices.

How much notice ends a monthly rental?

In URLTA counties, section 66-28-512 asks for written notice at least 30 days before the rent due date the notice names. A weekly rental needs ten days. For other counties the notices are 14, 30 and three day, so match the notice to your situation.

Can a Tennessee landlord charge a late fee?

In URLTA counties, yes, a fee of up to a tenth of the rent past due, and only after the five day grace period. The grace period does not count Sundays or legal holidays. No late fee cap is listed for other counties, so check your lease.

Does selling the house cancel the tenant's lease?

No statute says so. Section 66-28-305 only frees a seller from later liability after the tenant gets written notice and the deposit goes to the buyer. A local attorney or the clerk can tell you what notice your county expects before you end a lease.

How long does a Tennessee eviction take?

No single timeline is set. Posted service must happen at least six days before the hearing, continuances are limited to 15 days, and a tenant has ten days to appeal. If the tenant appeals without bond, the landlord can still obtain possession.

Which eviction notice a Tennessee landlord must give

It depends on the county and the reason. The state's landlord tenant eviction rules split Tennessee into counties under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (URLTA) and every other county, which falls under Tennessee Code Annotated 66-7-101 and following.

Where the rental sitsNotice periods
URLTA countyFourteen day, seven day for repeat violations, three day for violence, threats or unsanitary conditions
Any other county14 day, 30 day, 3 day

A waiver of notice for nonpayment is possible in URLTA counties, so read the lease before drafting the notice.

Which Tennessee counties follow the URLTA?

Nineteen counties follow the act: Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Greene, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Putnam, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson. A rental in Nashville, Memphis, Knoxville or Chattanooga lands in a URLTA county. A rental in a county outside that list uses the shorter set of rules in Title 66, Chapter 7.

In non-URLTA counties only four statutes actually apply: Section 109 on termination of tenancy, Section 110 on tenants with disabilities, Section 111 on service and support animals, and Section 112 on domestic abuse. Ask the clerk of the general sessions court in your county to confirm which set of rules applies before you serve a notice.

Extra rules for rent in a URLTA county

URLTA gives tenants a five day grace period, and Sundays and legal holidays do not count toward it. The maximum late fee is 10 percent. The act also covers security deposits, abandonment, essential services and the duties of both landlord and tenant.

  • Fourteen day notice, the first period.
  • Seven day notice for repeat violations.
  • Three day notice for violence, threats or unsanitary conditions.

A landlord who plans to sell an occupied rental should count the grace period before announcing a default, and should put the reason for the notice in writing, since the court holds the owner to the reasons stated.

How a detainer warrant moves through general sessions court

Eviction starts with a detainer warrant filed in general sessions court. Tennessee Code Annotated recognizes three types: forcible entry and detainer (29-18-102), forcible detainer (29-18-103) and unlawful detainer (29-18-104). The written notice matters in court, because the owner must rely on the reasons in the notice, and new misconduct after the notice calls for another notice.

Service rules shape what the judge can award. Personal service supports a money judgment. Service on an adult found in possession, service on a contractually named party, or posting can support possession only. For posting, the officer must attempt personal service on three different dates, record the attempts on the warrant, post a copy on the door and mail it, with the posting at least six days before the hearing.

Hearing delays and the tenant's right to appeal

A continuance is capped at 15 days unless the parties agree, the landlord consents or no court is being held. After judgment, a defendant may appeal within ten days under 29-18-129, giving bond, or seek certiorari and supersedeas in circuit court within thirty days. The certiorari route requires a meritorious reason and a bond covering costs, damages and the rent for the premises during the litigation.

  • When judgment goes to the plaintiff and a writ of possession is awarded, it is executed and the plaintiff restored to possession immediately.
  • If the defendant appeals without posting the bond for one year of rent, the landlord does not have to post a bond to obtain possession.
  • When a defendant appeals and does post, the landlord's bond must be double the value of one year's rent.

A landlord also earns interest on the judgment from the date of judgment if the tenant's appeal fails.

Serving a tenant who cannot be found

An "absent" defendant route exists. Personal service is dispensed with when the defendant is a nonresident, cannot be found and is believed to have left the state, the summons came back "not to be found in my county," the defendant's name or residence is unknown after diligent inquiry, or a domestic corporation has ceased doing business.

In those cases service by publication under Sections 21-1-203 through 21-1-205 applies, and the plaintiff must also post a copy of the publication notice on the front door or other front portion of the premises at least fifteen days before the date set for the defendant to appear. Keep a written record of each attempt to find the person.

Subsidized housing and domestic abuse survivors

Subsidized leases bring in a third party. HUD, THDA and Rural Development are the usual sources, with a three way agreement among landlord, HUD and tenant, and the lease may not contradict the tenancy addendum. Notice requirements for a subsidized unit can differ from state law, so the owner needs written notice that fits both sets of rules.

Domestic abuse has its own protections in both URLTA and non-URLTA counties. If domestic abuse is the underlying offense for ending a tenancy, only the perpetrator may be evicted, and victims, minor children and innocent occupants may not be. A tenant who is a domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking victim can ask in writing for release from the lease, with a release date agreed within 30 days and a copy of a valid order of protection or documents of a criminal charge.

Checklist before filing a detainer warrant

Run through these points in order. Each affects whether a judge can grant possession.

  • Confirm whether the county follows the URLTA or Title 66, Chapter 7.
  • Match the notice type and number of days to the reason for ending the tenancy.
  • Count the five day grace period for rent in a URLTA county, skipping Sundays and legal holidays.
  • Serve the warrant on an adult found in possession or on a named party to the lease, or document three attempts on different dates before posting.
  • Calendar the 15 day continuance limit, the ten day appeal period and the thirty day certiorari period.

A landlord who is also trying to sell should share this calendar with the buyer's agent so everyone plans around the same dates.

Eviction and selling a Tennessee rental house

An open detainer case, a recent notice and a tenant who may appeal all affect timing. A buyer who is financing may need vacant possession by closing, while an investor may accept the house with the tenant in place. A writ of possession is what restores the plaintiff to possession, and a defendant has ten days to appeal, so a sale contract that depends on vacancy needs a closing date that leaves room for both steps.

Bring the lease, every notice, the detainer warrant and the judgment to your title company or closing attorney. Ask the general sessions clerk in the county for the case status before you accept a closing date. A cash buyer can take the house with the tenant in place, which avoids waiting on the court calendar.

Frequently asked questions

How many days of notice must a Tennessee landlord give?

It depends on the county and the reason. URLTA counties use fourteen, seven and three day notices, and other counties use 14, 30 and 3 day notices. Check the lease and the notice type for your county.

Which Tennessee counties follow the URLTA?

Nineteen follow it: Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Greene, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Putnam, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson.

Does the tenant get a grace period?

In URLTA counties, yes. Tenants have five days, and Sundays and legal holidays do not count. The maximum late fee is 10 percent.

How fast can a landlord regain possession after winning?

Immediately once a writ of possession is awarded and executed. The defendant can still appeal within ten days or seek certiorari within thirty days, and the bond rules decide whether the landlord must wait.

Can a landlord evict a domestic abuse victim?

No, when domestic abuse is the underlying offense. Only the perpetrator may be evicted, and the landlord may not evict victims, minor children or innocent occupants.

Which Tennessee court handles an estate?

The court that exercises probate jurisdiction in the county where the person lived at death handles the estate. Tennessee statutes call this simply the court, and they define it by the decedent's legal residence on the date of death. The clerk of that county's court is the first call.

The first practical question for a family holding an inherited house is whether anyone has been appointed to act for the estate. Letters from that court show who is authorized to act for the estate, and limited letters name only the property listed in the petition. A buyer or title company may ask what authority you hold before closing.

Small estates in Tennessee

A small estate is a probate estate whose property does not exceed $50,000. The Small Estate Probate Act, Tennessee Code Title 30, Chapter 4, lets one or more competent adult heirs ask for limited letters instead of opening a full administration.

  • Waiting period: a petition can be filed after 45 days from the date of death, shown by the death certificate, if no one has filed a petition to appoint a personal representative in that time. The court can waive the wait for good cause.
  • Petition: a sworn petition lists each item of property, its value, each creditor and the amount owed.
  • Bond: a corporate surety bond equal to the property value is required, unless the petitioners are the sole heirs or sole beneficiaries, or all adult heirs and beneficiaries consent in writing.
  • Creditors: no notice to creditors is published, and creditors may not file claims in the small estate.
  • Closing: the limited letters stay open until the first anniversary of issuance, when the court automatically discharges the personal representative and surety.

A will can be used too. If the decedent left a will that distributes differently than intestacy would, the named personal representative may file it as a muniment of title, or record the original with the clerk along with witness affidavits, or two disinterested persons' affidavits for a handwritten will.

Can a small estate petition cover the house?

It cannot. The act defines property as personal property only, and the model limited letters state that no real property is at issue and that the letters give the personal representative no authority over real estate. A house or land therefore needs a different route.

If extra assets turn up that push the estate over $50,000, the court may allow the small estate to be converted to a full probate administration on a verified petition filed by the personal representative or a creditor. The people who received property earlier remain liable for what they were paid.

For an heir who wants to sell the home, the clerk of the probate court is the right place to ask what documents show authority over the deed. Bring the death certificate, any will, and a list of everyone who may have an interest in the property.

What small estate letters let you do with property

The personal representative collects and preserves the assets listed in the petition, removes personal property from a unit the decedent leased, and cancels insurance that no longer applies after the death. Anyone who owes the estate money, or holds estate property such as a bank, must pay or deliver it once shown a clerk-certified copy of the limited letters and receiving a demand. A person who hands property over in good faith is released from further liability to the estate and its creditors.

If a holder refuses, the property can be recovered, and a court can compel delivery, with costs charged to the person who wrongfully refused. Distribution then goes to the heirs as the law provides, or under the will if it was admitted as a muniment of title or recorded with the clerk. Know those limits before an heir spends money on the house: small estate letters reach vehicles, accounts and similar personal property, while the deed stays outside them.

What full administration involves

Full administration starts with letters testamentary if there is a will, or letters of administration if there is none.

  • Inventory: within 60 days after taking office, the personal representative must complete an accurate inventory of the probate estate and return it to the clerk, verified under oath.
  • Beneficiary notice: within the same 60 days, each legatee or devisee gets a copy of the will or the relevant paragraphs, and each residuary distributee of an intestate estate gets a copy of the letters of administration.
  • Notice to creditors: within 30 days after letters are issued, the clerk publishes two consecutive weekly notices in a county newspaper, or posts written notices in three public places if the county has no newspaper.
  • Claims: creditors must file by the earlier of the dates in the notice, which includes 12 months from the date of death, or their claims are forever barred.
  • Exceptions: until 30 days after four months from the notice, the personal representative or an interested party may except to a claim in writing.

A house can sit in an estate for most of a year. Ask the clerk which dates apply to your file, because the notice sets them. A cash buyer can close once the signer has proper authority, but the court's dates still apply.

Small estate and full administration compared

If the estate holds a house, the full administration column is the one that applies.

Small estate procedure and full administration in Tennessee.
FeatureSmall estateFull administration
Value limit$50,000 or lessNo limit
Real propertyNot coveredNot limited to personal property
Wait to file45 days after death, unless the court waives itTiming follows the appointment and the notice dates
Notice to creditorsNone publishedTwo weekly notices in a county newspaper
Claims barCreditors may not fileEarlier of the notice dates or 12 months from death
Court involvementLimited letters, open about one yearInventory and notices to the clerk

Debts that can follow an inherited house

Medical assistance is one debt that can reach beyond the estate. If property is distributed before all medical assistance owed to TennCare under Tennessee Code section 71-5-116 is paid, both the personal representative and the person receiving the property stay liable to TennCare, up to the value received. Anyone who plans to sell inherited property should ask the clerk or an attorney whether a TennCare claim exists before sharing proceeds.

Other debts matter too. Those who receive property from a small estate remain liable for up to one year after receiving it to unpaid creditors, to anyone with a prior right to the property, and to any personal representative appointed later.

Property taxes continue while a house waits in probate. Our Tennessee property tax guide explains the bill, the appeal calendar and the relief programs, and the county trustee can give a current balance for the parcel.

Frequently asked questions

How long does probate take in Tennessee?

The creditor claim period can run as long as 12 months from the date of death, which sets the pace of a full administration. A small estate stays open until the first anniversary of the limited letters. Ask the probate clerk for the dates in your own notice.

Can I sell an inherited house through the small estate procedure?

No. The small estate law covers personal property only, and the limited letters say they give no authority over real estate. A house needs another form of probate, so ask the clerk of the court in the county where the owner lived.

How soon can I file a small estate petition?

After 45 days from the date of death, as shown by a death certificate, unless someone has already filed to appoint a personal representative. The court may waive the 45 day wait for good cause shown.

Do creditors get notice in a small estate?

No. A notice to creditors must not be published and creditors are not permitted to file claims. Recipients of property still owe unpaid creditors for up to one year after receiving it.

What must a personal representative do within 60 days?

Complete and verify an inventory of the probate estate and return it to the clerk, and send beneficiaries a copy of the will or letters. The 60 days run from entering on the administration.

From delinquent tax suit to tax sale

Property taxes are due on the first Monday in October and turn delinquent on March 1 of the following year. After that, the county trustee can still collect the tax with penalty and interest, but only until the account is turned over to the delinquent tax attorney.

The attorney then files suit in chancery or circuit court after February 1 and before April 1. The complaint may name every delinquent taxpayer in the county, and the suit takes priority on the court's docket. Once a defendant pays the tax, interest, penalty and accrued court costs, the proceeding is dismissed as to that owner's property without any court order.

Two points matter to owners. A court has no authority to delay collection or to order payment in installments, even where more time would help the county. And a court keeps jurisdiction to collect the tax even if the assessment was wrong or the procedures were flawed, so an owner who thinks the assessment is wrong should not rely on the suit to fix it.

What happens at a tax sale

After judgment, the county holds a public sale of the parcel for cash, subject to the owner's equity of redemption. That term means the taxpayer can still pay the taxes, interest, penalties and costs and end the sale proceeding.

  • Advertisement: one notice in the newspaper, or printed handbills if the court orders, lists the owners, describes each parcel by deed book and page or property number, and states the amount of each judgment.
  • Mailed notice: certified return receipt mail goes to the owner's last known address in the assessor's records and to anyone else with an interest who can be found after a reasonable search.
  • Recorded notice: a version of the sale notice may be recorded with the register of deeds, for information only, with no release required.
  • Who may not buy: people with a duty to pay the taxes, fiduciaries of the taxpayer, and usually a spouse buying the other spouse's property.
  • County bid: the clerk bids the amount due if no one offers the same or more, except where the county legislative body has decided not to bid on environmentally risky or non-buildable parcels.

Sale proceeds first pay the delinquent tax attorney's compensation, then the costs of the suit, then the state, the county and the municipality in that order. If money remains, the person who got notice of the sale also gets notice of the proceeds, how they were divided and the remainder.

Redemption periods

The right to redeem vests in all interested persons when the court enters its order confirming the sale, and it can never be exercised more than one year after that date. The court sets the redemption period for each parcel before the sale and may restate it in the confirming order. The length depends on how long the taxes went unpaid.

Public Chapter 971 (Senate Bill 1983 and House Bill 1932) amends Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-2701(a)(1)(C) and adds a second scale. It applies to orders confirming a tax sale entered on or after July 1, 2026, so a sale confirmed this fall follows the newer schedule.

Tennessee redemption periods by years of delinquency
Order confirming sale enteredYears delinquentRedemption period
Before July 1, 2026Five or fewerOne year
Before July 1, 2026More than five, fewer than eight180 days
Before July 1, 2026Eight or more90 days
On or after July 1, 2026Three or fewerOne year
On or after July 1, 2026More than three90 days

A vacant or abandoned property can have a thirty-day period regardless of the number of delinquent years, where the court finds a reasonable basis to believe the property is vacant, or, for vacant land, abandoned.

What redeeming costs

Before filing the motion to redeem, the person redeeming pays the clerk the total delinquent taxes, penalty, interest and court costs, plus interest on the whole purchase price the buyer paid. That interest is 12 percent a year, running from the day the purchaser paid the clerk until the motion is filed. If the full amount is not paid on time, or the motion is not timely filed, the redemption fails.

  • The motion must describe the parcel, the sale date and the date of the order confirming the sale, and state why the filer has a right to redeem.
  • Within ten days after the filing and payment, the clerk sends notice to the purchaser and to everyone entitled to redeem.
  • The purchaser has thirty days after the notice is mailed to ask for additional money to cover the amounts it spent on the property.
  • Additional funds ordered by the court are due by the later of the end of the redemption period or thirty days after the order.

When redemption is completed, title is divested out of the purchaser and the clerk refunds the purchase money. The owner's interest returns to the position it held when the sale was confirmed. A lienholder who redeems may then proceed to foreclose.

Can a buyer purchase the right to redeem?

A transferee can bring a motion to redeem, but the statute guards against profiteering. The court must deny the motion if the tax sale purchaser or another interested party objects and it appears the transferee is speculating. Speculation is presumed when the right of redemption was transferred for less than the purchase price at the tax sale minus what the debtor would have paid to redeem. The court may award attorney's fees to the party who successfully challenges the motion.

For an owner thinking of selling, a buyer who pays real money for the house itself, and who pays off the taxes, is in a different position from someone buying only a redemption right at a discount.

Selling before a tax sale

Until the sale, the owner holds title and can sell. Paying the tax, interest, penalty and costs ends the suit as to that parcel, so a closing that pays the balance clears the proceeding. If the account is still with the trustee, the trustee must accept the delinquent tax with penalty and interest.

  • Ask the county trustee for the current balance, or the delinquent tax attorney's office if the suit has been filed.
  • Ask the clerk of the chancery or circuit court whether a sale date has been set.
  • Give the title company the payoff figure so it can be paid at closing.

A cash sale can close quickly enough to beat a sale date, since there is no lender underwriting to wait on. After the sale, a different timeline controls. The owner's interest is subject to the redemption period, and a sale of the house during that window has to deal with the purchaser's position and the clerk's records. An attorney can sequence that step.

Frequently asked questions

When do Tennessee property taxes become delinquent?

On March 1 of the year after the first Monday in October due date. The trustee keeps accepting payment with penalty and interest until the account goes to the delinquent tax attorney.

When is the delinquent tax suit filed?

After February 1 and before April 1, in chancery or circuit court, by the delinquent tax attorney.

What is the interest rate to redeem a property sold at tax sale?

Twelve percent a year on the purchaser's full purchase price, from the day the purchaser pays the clerk until the motion to redeem is filed, plus the delinquent taxes, penalty, interest and court costs.

How long is the redemption period for a sale confirmed in 2026?

For orders confirming a sale on or after July 1, 2026, it is one year if the delinquency was three years or less and 90 days if it was longer, under Public Chapter 971. A vacant or abandoned property can have a 30-day period.

Who gets the money left over after a Tennessee tax sale?

Proceeds pay the attorney, then costs, then the state, county and municipality. If anything remains, notice of the remainder goes to the person who received the sale notice.
